title: What is occupational therapy | NHS inform
text:
What is occupational therapy
Occupational therapy supports people who find it difficult to take part in occupations (the activities that matter to them). This may be due to disability, their physical health, mental health, environment or social circumstances.
An occupational therapist will work with you to find ways to do what’s important to you. This could be everyday tasks like getting dressed. It could also be activities that support your health and wellbeing like:
looking after your children
going to work
taking part in education
doing your hobbies
going out
Many different techniques and equipment can be used as part of occupational therapy. Sometimes you may need a change in your environment.
Your occupational therapist will discuss your options. They’ll work with you to find ways to help maintain, regain or improve your independence and participation in daily activities.
Equipment
Depending on your needs, occupational therapists may suggest tools or equipment you may find helpful like:
apps and digital tools to help your memory
specialist seating, beds and hoists
a walking stick, walking frame or wheelchair
electric can openers
tap turners
kettle tippers
two-handled cups
cutlery with large handles
an adapted computer keyboard or mouse
voice-controlled lights or software
Tell your occupational therapist about any difficulties you have. No matter how small they seem, there may be equipment that can help.
Equipment cost
If your occupational therapist thinks you need equipment to help you, you can usually get it for free on a long-term loan. However, different local authorities may charge for some pieces of equipment.
Equipment for work
If you need equipment to help you carry out your work, the
Access to Work scheme
may be able to provide funding.
Contact the disability employment adviser at your local
Jobcentre Plus
for advice and help.
Buying your own equipment
You may choose to buy your own equipment rather than use the equipment provided by your local council.
If you’re going to buy your own equipment, it’s still a good idea to have an assessment by an occupational therapist. They can explain what equipment is most suitable and tell you what’s available.
Getting equipment on loan
You might need some equipment on a short-term basis. For example, if someone with a disability is visiting you.
Your local
British Red Cross
can often lend wheelchairs and other equipment for short periods of time.
Adapting your environment
Occupational therapy may involve making an environment suitable for your needs. This could be your home, workplace or where you’re studying.
It may involve changes like:
putting in ramps to allow access in a wheelchair
fitting a stairlift
installing grab rails by the stairs
providing a raised toilet seat, bath lift or shower seat
clearing up clutter, reorganising cupboards
providing visual cues so you can safely move around and reach what you need
The cost of adaptations to your house
If you need adaptations to your house, these may be carried out free of charge. However, this will depend on your local authority. If you rent you’ll need the permission of your landlord.
Larger, more expensive items and major adaptations may be managed by the housing department. You may also need to contribute towards the cost of these items.
Grants may be available to help with the cost of adaptations. You should contact your local authority to find out if you’re eligible for these grants. The amount paid by a grant will depend on your income and outgoings.
The Scottish Government has more information on
funding adaptations
.
Activity grading
Activity grading is a way of breaking down an activity into more manageable steps. An occupational therapist may use this to help you take part in an activity. For example, if your goal is to walk to work, but it’s too far for you to do at once, this can be broken down.
On your first day, you could get the bus most of the way and then walk the last part. Each week, you could get off the bus a stop earlier and increase the distance you walk.
As you become more confident with an activity, you can progress to the next stage. Eventually you’ll reach your goal.
Graded exposure
Graded exposure is like activity grading. However, it’s more focused on dealing with the emotional and psychological side of rehabilitation.
Graded exposure is used to help gradually build your confidence. It can help establish meaningful routines that you may otherwise avoid.
Workplace rehabilitation
Workplace rehabilitation means helping someone with physical, psychological and/or social difficulties to return to or remain in work. It’s also sometimes called vocational rehabilitation.
Work includes jobs that aren’t paid, like being a full-time parent or a volunteer.
An occupational therapist can help by:
assessing your workplace
assessing your role at work
assessing your ability to complete work activities, and finding ways to assist you
finding ways to manage your condition while at work
providing extra training
finding a way to cope with problems like discrimination and prejudice
helping your employers manage your return to work
increasing awareness of your condition
monitoring your progress
completing
fit notes
where appropriate
Leisure rehabilitation
Taking part in leisure activities can stop you feeling isolated because of your condition. It can also improve your quality of life. While you need to be able to care for yourself and work, being able to take part in activities for fun is also important.
An occupational therapist may discuss what activities you enjoy. They’ll find practical ways to help you continue doing those activities.
For example, if you like going to the shops but find it tiring, they may suggest a wheeled walker with a seat and basket.
If you enjoy gardening but find some tasks difficult, they can identify easier ways of carrying out those tasks. You may need to use different techniques and specially adapted gardening tools.
Occupational therapists can also help if your mental health impacts your leisure activities. They may work with you to improve your motivation, concentration and energy levels.
Thinking about activities differently
An occupational therapist will look at the activity you’re finding difficult. They’ll then see if there’s another way to do it.
For example, if you find it difficult to peel and chop vegetables, you could buy pre-prepared vegetables. There may also be a small piece of equipment to help with chopping and peeling.
If you’re finding if difficult to manage fatigue, you may agree with your employer to work flexible hours and to factor in regular breaks to your day.

Royal College of Occupational Therapists
